item.title: Strangely Specific Signs of Social Anxiety
item.description:
There comes a time in everyone’s life when they must confront the thing that makes them most anxious. This might be traveling by airplane, having to address a room of hundreds of people, or, for those with social anxiety, it might be something as simple as answering the phone. The signs of social anxiety can be so unexpected that it’s easy to be dismissive of someone’s struggle.

People with social anxiety frequently think of themselves as introverted or even quirky because they haven’t found a sufficient explanation for their anxieties. Whatever is happening beneath the surface, it is something that can be resolved. It may feel debilitating now, but it doesn’t have to stay that way.

Imperfect Comparisons

How often do we look at our peers and marvel at their confidence, tenacity, or success? We might envy their communication skills or their ability to hold the attention of the entire room when they speak. We can’t see their anxiety each time they speak, or the long road they have taken to find success.

It’s fine to compare ourselves to others if it inspires us to improve certain things. However, comparison so often makes us feel worse about ourselves, even when we can’t see things like hidden social anxiety.

Outwardly, a person might not display any signs of social anxiety, but just because we cannot see it does not mean it isn’t there. Perhaps they spent decades confronting their fears before they reached the point where they could confidently communicate with crowds. It’s not a bad idea to aspire to have someone else’s levels of confidence or communication skills. Keep in mind, though, that people are like icebergs; only a small part of them is visible.

Filling in the Gaps

Our brains have a wonderful ability to fill in the gaps when it comes to things we don’t understand or can’t fully see. This is how we make assumptions about others: our brain takes the information presented to it and guesses the rest.

Sometimes we are correct in our assumptions. It’s safe to assume that the person who is the life and soul of a party simply loves the limelight. However, what if that person is deeply depressed and doing an excellent job of covering up? Sometimes the root of our social anxiety lies in the mistaken assumptions our brains have made about ourselves and others.

For example, on a date, there are awkward moments of silence. This is normal and doesn’t necessarily mean anything bad. However, your brain might convince you that your date is quiet because he finds you boring. The truth is likely that they are quiet because they are also making assumptions about you.

In psychology, this is called a cognitive distortion. It is when a person’s brain habitually fills in the gaps in faulty ways. There are different kinds of cognitive distortions, but almost all of them are related to social anxiety.

When we assume that we know what others think about us, that is a cognitive distortion known as mind-reading. Expecting the worst possible outcome to every situation is a cognitive distortion known as catastrophizing, and taking the blame for things that couldn’t possibly be our fault is personalization.

Treating Social Anxiety

Social anxiety is more complicated than other forms of anxiety because of the cognitive distortions that are layered into it. We experience the physical effects of general anxiety, like the elevated heartbeat, sweaty hands and back, and shallow breathing.

We also experience emotional turmoil related to cognitive distortions, like having low self-worth, being easily embarrassed, and feeling exposed and insecure. This means that each person with social anxiety has any number of cognitive distortions fueling their fears. To treat the anxiety, you must get to the root of each distortion and challenge it.

Unfortunately, many people instinctively treat their social anxiety through avoidance, by rehearsing conversations before having them, or by ruminating on events once they are passed. Avoiding a party, for example, is another way of saying, “I’m not going because I know I would be judged by everyone there.”

Cognitive distortions sound so confident and assured, and avoidance behaviors, or ruminating and rehearsing behaviors, give the distortions too much weight. If you had confronted your thinking and attended the party, you would have given your brain the chance to calm down and prove to it that there was no real threat. It’s a complicated process to treat social anxiety, but perhaps the place to start is learning to recognize it.

Noticing the Signs of Social Anxiety

The majority of people who classify themselves as shy or introverted actually have untreated social anxiety. When we begin to see the signs of social anxiety in ourselves, we can begin to challenge the cognitive distortions behind them. The signs of social anxiety are often a combination of a cognitive distortion and an anxious action.

For example, people with social anxiety frequently cancel their plans at the last moment. This is avoidance behavior that usually stems from overthinking. The person wants to make their friends happy, so they initially agree to any and every suggestion. Meanwhile, they start catastrophizing or feeling the pressure to be perfect in a social situation, and they can’t face the pressure.

Just like with general anxiety, one of the clear signs of social anxiety is nervous fidgeting. The person gets a build-up of nervous energy and needs to discharge it with physical activity. There is no cognitive distortion attached to this behavior; it is simply a form of self-soothing.

Social anxiety is almost always visible in a person’s body language or speech, but most frequently it shows up as uncontrollable blushing. Whenever the person feels the spotlight on them, even by way of ordinary eye contact or polite interest, blood rushes to their face, and they can’t help but blush. Others might find it endearing, but for the person who can’t control their blushing, it is a physical nightmare.

One of the most common cognitive distortions related to social anxiety is the unshakable belief that others find you awkward or dull. Once again, this is mind-reading: you believe you know exactly what others think of you. Unfortunately, when you believe others find you awkward or uninteresting, your body language begins to stiffen, you avoid eye contact, and you forget how to interact naturally, making you come across as strange or cold.

On the topic of body language, people with social anxiety are usually found huddling on the outskirts of the group, with their shoulders hunched and jaws clenched. They are literally trying to shrink down their presence to avoid being noticed. There could be any number of cognitive distortions behind thinking like this, but it is almost certain that some kind of wrong thinking is inflating their social anxiety.

Lastly, one of the most common signs of social anxiety is that people stay on the move. They go from one group to the next, never staying long enough to be drawn into a conversation, and always hanging on the outskirts. They make sure that they never settle because their instinct is to escape the situation. Much like fidgeting, they are turning their nervous energy into motion and movement.

Truth and Freedom

Social anxiety is complex, but it is treatable. Our cognitive distortions might inflate the perceived threats in our heads, but it is possible to confront these thoughts and challenge them. When we do that, we begin to see and understand things as they truly are, not as we believed them to be. As the Scripture confirms, when we know the truth, it will set us free. (John 8:32) You are only as restricted by social anxiety as you allow yourself to be; freedom is waiting for you.

It’s not always easy to recognize the signs of social anxiety, much less confront the beliefs behind it. If you would like support navigating these challenges, I invite you to contact my office to schedule a session with me, Joseph Bennett, MAMFC, MARE, LPC. My team is warm, welcoming, and happy to make the process feel easy and comfortable from the first conversation.

item.title: When to Seek Binge-Eating Treatment
item.description:
Binge-eating disorder is a serious mental health condition that typically requires professional counseling to work through, but it is possible to overcome the eating disorder. However, people often miss the signs or wait too long to seek binge-eating treatment.

Know the signs of binge-eating disorder, take your treatment seriously, and lean on your faith in God and His Son, Jesus Christ, and you will take your life back.

What are the signs of binge-eating disorder?

Sometimes the line between overeating (which many people do throughout the year) and binge-eating becomes blurred. Overeating may or may not be intentional and is typically contained in a single meal.

Binge-eating, however, can happen during a span of two hours. During a binge, you may consume hundreds or thousands of calories with no sensation of your stomach being full. Worse, you may zone out during the binge and suddenly realize what you have done hours later.

Do any of these signs of binge-eating disorder sound familiar?

  • Do you binge on food in a short period of time?
  • Do you keep your binges a secret?
  • Do you feel sick, ashamed, guilty, or distressed after a binge?
  • Do you frequently zone out during a binge?
  • Do you binge often?

If you answered yes to most of these questions, it might be time to seek treatment.

Do I need treatment?

The best indicator of whether you need treatment is your emotions after a binge. Do you feel ashamed or guilty? Are you depressed and feel like your life is out of control? These are the mental aspects of an eating disorder.

What about the physical complications from bingeing? Your primary care physician will complete bloodwork and a physical exam to rule out any medical conditions related to the bingeing behavior before diagnosing. Bingeing can lead to obesity, joint pain, digestive issues, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and other grave conditions.

Once you know that you need treatment, you can begin to proactively make lifestyle changes even before your first appointment with a specialist. The following is a list of some of our top tips:

Be mindful of hunger An episode of binge-eating may or may not happen when you are hungry. However, being aware of your hunger cues can help you be mindful of when you are reaching the point when your stomach is full.

Has it been a few hours since you last ate? Is your stomach growling or feeling empty? If your last meal consisted of unhealthy junk foods, your blood sugar might crash, leaving you dizzy, lightheaded, and faint. This can set you up for a binge to counteract the effects of low blood sugar.

Know your trigger foods and emotions If your emotions are running high, they can trigger a binge. Feeling stressed, overwhelmed, lonely, sad, hurt, or angry can leave you wanting something to take away the emotion.

You are looking for a way to fill your heart, but instead of turning to God and his word, you reach (sometimes unconsciously) for comfort food. If you find yourself bingeing on the same foods every time, consider removing those foods from your home until you feel confident in your treatment and more in control.

Slow down and focus When you catch yourself in the pantry, refrigerator, or car looking for a place to grab a quick bite, stop and consider your surroundings and mood. Are you actually hungry, or are you trying to avoid a particular emotion?

When you sit down to eat, eliminate all distractions to avoid zoning out during the meal. Turn off your phone, television, and other screens and focus on the portion in front of you. If you must eat in the car, pack your meal in a portion-controlled container.

Journal your food intake Sometimes change is preceded by an “ah-ha” moment, the moment you realize that you must change or else. There is something powerful in the “ah-ha” moment. It propels you to make better choices, learn new things, and stop making excuses.

Journaling your daily meals and snacks could be your “ah-ha” moment. Forcing yourself to write down every bite during a binge could be the eye-opener you need to make a change. Jot down your mood when the binge began and how you felt afterward. Analyzing your emotions can lead to a breakthrough.

Plan your meals Bingeing leaves you feeling out of control. If you sit down once a week and plan out your meals and snacks (leaving it flexible), you are more likely to stick to the plan, even on the busiest days. Knowing you have something good to look forward to every few hours may head off a binge. Plan to eat every three to four hours to keep your blood sugar constant.

Train your body When you exercise, your appetite decreases as hunger hormones shift. If the word exercise gives you images of leotard-clad women bouncing around to aerobics music, then think of it as training your body.

God wants us to train both our physical body to keep it fit and ready for His service, and our spiritual body. “Physical training is good, but training for godliness is much better, promising benefits in this life and in the life to come.” (1 Timothy 4:8 NLT)

These are a few activities you can try before and during binge-eating treatment. But once you agree to an appointment with an eating disorder therapist, what can you expect during your sessions?

What can I expect from binge-eating treatment?

Each client is unique, and we tailor our treatment plans to meet your needs. Some of the therapies listed below will not pertain to your treatment plan, but others will become the foundation of your recovery with Jesus Christ as the cornerstone.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) – CBT has been proven to be beneficial in helping people with mental conditions across the board, from anxiety and depression to Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder to eating disorders.

CBT works with the negative thoughts that run through our minds before a binge. It teaches us how to catch those thoughts and change the verbiage, thus changing the resulting behavioral pattern. Since bingeing is, in part, a condition based on the behavior, changing the thoughts preceding the binge should change the binge-eating behavior.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) – DBT works to make the client aware of the present moment and stop zoning out, particularly during a binge. The therapy also uses the client’s tolerance by slowly increasing it, so they learn to face their emotions head-on instead of escaping from them. DBT is used to teach clients communication skills for conflict resolution.

Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) – IPT focuses on the communication and relationship issues that may be affecting the client and possibly at the root of the eating disorder. When we have problems in our relationships, it can result in psychological problems and negative behaviors. IPT gets to the origin of these issues and uses new problem-solving skills to strengthen relationships and resolve conflicts.

Group Counseling – Group counseling provides support, advice, encouragement, and psychological techniques. Clients feel safe in smaller groups to share with others dealing with binge-eating and various eating disorders. Each session is confidential and hosted by a licensed counselor.

Each of our counselors treats binge-eating disorder in their own way and personalizes their treatments to the client. However, you always have a say in how you feel about a particular treatment strategy.

When You Need Treatment

The first step to overcoming binge-eating is realizing you need help. The second step is seeking assistance in breaking the cycle of this severe eating disorder before it leads to physical and mental illnesses.

Reach out to one of our counselors today to discuss diagnosis and treatment options. Even if you have tried counseling before, give us a call. We customize your treatment plan while helping you grow in your faith and relationship with Jesus. Together, we can beat binge-eating disorder.

item.title: Living with ADHD and Emotional Regulation Challenges at Work
item.description:
People usually think ADHD only means trouble with focus, getting distracted, forgetting tasks, or jumping from one thing to another. But for many adults with this misunderstood condition, emotions play just as big a role, especially with workplace challenges.

You see, a person with ADHD doesn’t just deal with attention difficulties. They experience emotions more intensely, react impulsively, and struggle to manage frustration, rejection, or stress. These emotional difficulties affect motivation, work relationships, and how much someone gets done.

When people understand ADHD and emotional regulation, it becomes easier to find helpful coping tips that help.

What Emotional Regulation Means in ADHD

Emotional regulation is a technical phrase to describe how someone manages their feelings. For people with ADHD, it feels like every emotion comes on strong, especially when something unexpected happens that can trigger an immediate emotional response before there’s time to process it. It could just be an email that changes their plans, a comment from a coworker, or a small mistake.

This makes you feel anger, shame, or disappointment before they even have time to think. Once these feelings hit, they can stay with you; then one irritating thing from the morning might be running in your mind all afternoon.

Feedback can feel personal, even when it’s meant to help. You may shut down or feel like you did something wrong. This doesn’t mean you’re too sensitive. You’re reacting in a way that makes sense for your brain.

Over time, this makes you feel drained, although you’re not physically tired, but rather more emotionally tired because everything takes more energy. When you understand how ADHD affects your emotions at work, things start to make more sense.

How Emotions Change the Way You Work

Putting Things Off When You’re Overwhelmed Tasks feel harder when you’re already frustrated. Starting them means facing that feeling, so you end up procrastinating. Then stress builds, and it becomes harder to start.

Losing Motivation A small problem, a missed meeting, a mean message, a tech issue – anything can feel like a big failure. That drops your drive to keep going.

Communication Trouble When emotions are high, it’s hard to talk things out. You quickly snap, shut down, or pull back, and that creates confusion with coworkers.

Emotional Fatigue By the end of each workday, you feel extraordinarily empty. Even simple things feel like too much.

These aren’t lazy habits, but all those constant emotional difficulties drain your energy, making it harder to stay productive long-term. Finding the underlying cause of these patterns in your life helps create better strategies for managing emotions at work.

Sadly, most advice for ADHD focuses on time or focus tools. Those help, but they also miss a big part of it all, which is how emotions affect your day and why you need to pay more attention to them.

If no one talks about how emotions should be regulated, especially for someone with ADHD, you’re left feeling like you’re failing. But sometimes all you need are the right tools that fit how your brain works. Those important tools are easy to try out and don’t take a lot of time. Eventually, they help you feel steadier at work.

Simple Tools to Help Manage Emotions Better at Work

Always pause before reacting When something upsets you, stop for a few seconds. Take a breath, stretch, and walk to get some water. Give yourself a short break to reset your emotions before replying or speaking.

Check in with yourself Set reminders to check in with emotions throughout the day. Ask, “Am I feeling overwhelmed? Do I need a break?” This helps you notice emotions before they take over.

Create a reset habit When emotions feel overwhelming, have a go-to reset strategy. Pick something that helps you calm down: a song, a quick walk, a stretch, or doing a quick physical activity. Use this after a stressful moment to clear your head.

Change harsh self-talk Instead of thinking, “I messed up,” change that to, “What can I learn from this?” Changing the way emotions are processed helps reduce frustration. Focus on the next move, not the mistake.

Watch your energy Watch out for which tasks drain you more, be it meetings, emails, or certain people. If certain conversations or tasks trigger stress, try to do them at times when you have more energy. Save lighter work for later in the day.

Write instead of speaking If a topic feels emotional, write it out in a message or email first. Writing gives you space to think, cool down, and process thoughts before responding.

Group tasks by feelings Some tasks trigger frustration more than others. Organizing work based on emotional energy helps manage reactions better. Put tough or frustrating tasks earlier in the day, then follow them with something easy or more fun to help you reset.

Be kind to yourself ADHD makes emotional regulation harder, but that doesn’t mean failure. Being kind to yourself helps reduce emotional stress. Give yourself credit for trying, and that helps more than being tough on yourself.

These handy tools and life tips won’t make your life perfect, but using them every day builds more strength over time.

Testimonies From Real People Who’ve Dealt with This

Many people with ADHD we’ve spoken to here on this site have shared how mixing emotional regulation with time management has helped them over the years.

One lady shared this: “I used to avoid feedback because it felt personal. Then I started pausing before responding and writing drafts of my replies. It helped me feel calmer and less like I was failing.”

Another shared this: “When I get overwhelmed on tough days, I’ve learnt the importance of having a backup hobby ready for me or going for a walk. It’s not that I’m ignoring work, but more of resetting my emotions so I can come back sane.”

And there are many more of these stories that show that emotional breaks and resets can make a real difference in a work setting.

How Managers and Coworkers Can Help with Emotional Regulation

You don’t have to carry the whole burden yourself. If your workplace is open to it, here are ways others can help with emotional regulation and ADHD:

  • Give short breaks in meetings for emotional reset time.
  • Offer feedback in writing to reduce real-time emotional reactions.
  • Check in after tough tasks or projects.

If you’re new to thinking about how your emotions can be managed better at work, start small. Pick one or two strategies, like pausing for a breath or opting for an email first, and try it for a week. Notice what changes. Do you feel less reactive? Less drained?

Then add another habit, like a midday reset, a note to check your mood. Little steps lead to big shifts over time.

Every day will still have emotional highs and lows. You’ll slip, and you’ll have a day when emotions win. That’s just part of ADHD that you should come to accept. Notice it, learn from it, then try again tomorrow.

Emotional regulation at work isn’t about fixing yourself. It makes you understand how your brain and emotions work together. It’s about respecting the ways feelings affect energy, communication, and what you get done.

With time, empathy for yourself, and support from others, work becomes a place you can handle, and even love, not just push through.

If you have ADHD or know that your emotions at work always feel hard or overwhelming, there is something that can be done to help you work through that. Many experts, coaches, and therapists understand this mix of focus and feeling.

You deserve a work life that doesn’t wear you out, and finding better ways to manage emotions healthily is a powerful start. If work still feels too hard emotionally, that’s not something to hide. Talking to a therapist, coach, or counselor can help. They understand ADHD and emotional regulation and know what tools work. Asking for help means you care about feeling better.

Reach out to a professional on this site who can help you today.
